title: Ellicott Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Ellicott wells have a 160-foot median depth, with drilling and a finished system commonly costing $14,000-$23,200.
h1: Ellicott, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land near Ellicott means evaluating the well record, not just the view from the lot. Within about five miles, Colorado DWR records show 1,468 permitted wells, including 748 recorded as constructed. Among the wells that report results, the median depth is 160 feet and the median reported yield is 11.7 gallons per minute.

Those figures are useful for planning, but they are not a guarantee for one parcel. Ellicott-area wells reach several named or unnamed aquifers, and the local record includes both shallow and much deeper holes. Check nearby permits, water rights, septic options, and the exact building site before you commit.

sections.heading: Ellicott well depths and the Denver Basin ground
sections.html:
Ellicott wells have a median reported depth of 160 feet. The middle half runs from 115 to 355 feet, so a driller bidding a new well should not treat the median as a fixed target. Most recorded wells, 58%, fall between 100 and 300 feet. Another 18% are between 300 and 600 feet, while 8% exceed 600 feet. The deepest record reaches 1,110 feet.

The ground is described in the cost model as Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. Permits identify Denver Basin aquifer wells throughout this area, with 686 wells associated with unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, 228 with the Arapahoe, and 211 with Quaternary Alluvium. Nearby results in Yoder, Falcon, Peyton, or other surrounding areas can provide context, but the closest wells to your lot matter most.

sections.heading: What an Ellicott well is likely to produce
sections.html:
Reported well yield is strong in this record, with a median of 11.7 gallons per minute and a middle half from 10.0 to 14.1 gallons per minute. Seventy-two percent of wells reporting yield fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 25% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Only 3% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and none report under 1 gallon per minute.

That does not mean every new hole will match the median. Only 384 wells report a pump yield, compared with 1,468 permitted wells overall. Ask for the neighboring well completion reports, pumping information, and any production test. A good yield still needs suitable storage, pump sizing, and water quality for the home you plan to build.

sections.heading: Ellicott water levels and the record over time
sections.html:
Among 113 wells reporting static water level, the median depth to water is 123 feet. The middle half is 81 to 198 feet below the surface. That depth affects casing, pump setting, electrical work, and the amount of trenching or equipment needed during construction.

The decade medians show deeper reported water levels over time: 28 feet in the 1950s, 65 feet in the 1960s, 145 feet in the 2010s, and 170 feet in the 2020s. This pattern suggests water was measured deeper in the more recent records, but it is not proof of a uniform decline. The wells, locations, aquifers, and measurement conditions may differ. A buyer should obtain the current static level and pumping information for the specific well rather than rely only on the historical series.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Ellicott, and when
sections.html:
Permit activity spans the area’s older rural development through current construction. Records show 36 permits from the 1950s, 79 from the 1960s, 124 from the 1970s, 239 from the 1980s, 200 from the 1990s, 233 from the 2000s, 98 from the 2010s, and 95 from the 2020s. The newest permit year in the record is 2025.

The most active listed drillers are Kunau Drilling LLC, with 256 records; M & B Drilling Co., with 207; and Hamacher Well Works Inc., with 171. Those counts describe permit records, not a guarantee of current availability or workmanship. Confirm licensing, insurance, scheduling, casing and grout specifications, testing, and exactly what the bid includes before selecting a contractor.

sections.heading: What a new Ellicott well may cost
sections.html:
The local drilling model uses a rate of $50 to $70 per foot for the Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 160-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $8,000 to $11,200. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $14,000 to $23,200.

Use the 115-to-355-foot middle-half depth range when comparing bids. A price based only on the median may be too low for a parcel that resembles the deeper nearby wells. Get a written allowance for mobilization, casing, grout, development, water testing, disposal, and difficult access. Confirm whether the quoted number covers only drilling or the complete usable water system.

sections.heading: Ellicott risks: water quality, dry holes, and septic layout
sections.html:
Low yield is not the main warning in the reported results, but incomplete reporting means the record cannot eliminate dry-hole or poor-production risk at a particular lot. Fractured-bedrock conditions can be unpredictable, and a nearby successful well does not guarantee the same result. Require a clear drilling and testing plan before work begins.

Environmental review also matters. Within about ten miles, the map shows 7 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 34 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not establish contamination at your property, but it supports testing the finished well for the contaminants relevant to the site and its land use. Keep the well, septic system, leach field, drive, and house location coordinated. Confirm El Paso County and state setbacks, septic approval, and the permit’s allowed household, stock, or irrigation use.

sections.heading: A practical Ellicott lot-buying and building check
sections.html:
Start with the closest permitted wells, not a countywide average. Review their depths, aquifers, static levels, yields, construction details, and use. The local permit mix is 67% domestic or household, 29% stock, 19% irrigation, and 4% monitoring, so confirm that a neighboring record is comparable to the home you want.

Before closing, make the well permit and completion record part of the inspection file. Test the existing water, verify pump performance, locate the septic system, and ask an experienced driller to price a replacement or new well using nearby depths. If you are building, confirm access for the rig and delivery equipment, then coordinate well, septic, driveway, utilities, and the house pad. In an over-appropriated basin, ask the water attorney or county about augmentation and the permitted use before assuming a domestic well solves every water need.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Ellicott, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Ellicott is 160 feet. The middle half runs from 115 to 355 feet, while 16% are under 100 feet and 8% exceed 600 feet. The deepest record is 1,110 feet. Those ranges are useful for budgeting, but the nearest comparable wells and aquifer records are more important for a specific lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Ellicott?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 160-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $8,000 to $11,200. A finished well including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $14,000 to $23,200. A deeper-than-median site, difficult access, or extra construction requirements can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Ellicott wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 11.7 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 14.1 gallons per minute. Seventy-two percent of reporting wells produce 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 25% report more than 15. Only 384 wells report a yield, so these results describe the record rather than guaranteeing a new well.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Ellicott?
faq.a: The permit map does not prove that any individual well is safe or unsafe to drink. It shows 7 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 34 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about ten miles. Test an existing or new well, especially for contaminants relevant to the property, and repeat testing after construction or changes in nearby land use.

faq.q: Are Ellicott well water levels getting lower?
faq.a: Reported static water levels are deeper in newer decade records: 28 feet in the 1950s, 65 feet in the 1960s, 145 feet in the 2010s, and 170 feet in the 2020s. That suggests deeper measured water levels over time, but it does not prove a uniform decline because locations, aquifers, wells, and measurement conditions differ. Check the specific well’s current level.
